annotations.keyFindings: Awakening trials were performed on 44 percent of 5,940 eligible days; overnight agitation and procedures were the commonest reasons, and a bedside checklist unit reached 58 percent against 37 percent.
annotations.limitations: Documentation-based; three units; no causal comparison of the checklist.

annotations.keyFindings: A shared 08:00 time and a bedside hand-off card raised paired trials from 22 to 49 percent of eligible days, with median ventilator days from 6.1 to 5.2.
The longest wait was physician approval (median 47 minutes); removing it for patients passing the screen raised completed interruptions from 35 to 63 percent over 16 weeks.
Nurses described fear of self-extubation, family presence, pressure before rounds and unclear authority as reasons not to interrupt sedation.
Self-extubation occurred in 0.6 percent of 4,200 interruptions, no more often than on non-interruption days; agitation needing a bolus occurred in 9 percent.
annotations.limitations: Nurse-recorded events; possible under-reporting on non-interruption days.

annotations.keyFindings: Daily interruption was associated with fewer ventilator days in trials (mean difference -1.2 days), where adherence was about 80 percent, against 30 to 55 percent in routine practice.
annotations.limitations: Implementation strategies rarely described; mixed designs.

annotations.keyFindings: An electronic reminder raised documented screening from 62 to 88 percent but completed interruptions only from 36 to 39 percent.
annotations.limitations: One unit; interrupted time series without a control series.

claims.text: In one unit's value stream, the longest wait was physician approval (median 47 minutes), and removing it for patients who passed the safety screen raised completed interruptions from 35 to 63 percent over 16 weeks.
claims.passage: the longest being physician approval before a nurse could stop sedation (median 47 minutes)
claims.interpretation: Waits for authority, not the screen itself, may be where the morning process breaks down.

claims.text: An electronic reminder raised documented screening from 62 to 88 percent while completed interruptions moved only from 36 to 39 percent.
claims.passage: documented screening rose from 62 percent to 88 percent of eligible days, but completed interruptions changed little, from 36 percent to 39 percent
claims.interpretation: A reminder is unlikely to help this unit, whose screen rate is already 71 percent.

claims.text: Self-extubation occurred in 0.6 percent of 4,200 nurse-driven interruptions and was not more frequent than on days without interruption.
claims.passage: Self-extubation occurred in 0.6 percent of interruptions
claims.interpretation: Self-extubation is the right balancing measure and is rare enough to need a days-between-events chart.

claims.text: A shared 08:00 time for awakening and breathing trials raised paired trials from 22 to 49 percent of eligible patient-days.
claims.passage: the proportion of eligible patient-days with a paired trial rose from 22 percent to 49 percent
claims.interpretation: Coordination with respiratory therapy is a countermeasure worth testing for the paired trial rate of 29 percent.

synthesis: Seven retrieved records from the second search, appraised at abstract level; the first search reported two hits but returned no records, and three model leads remain unchecked. Routine adherence to sedation interruption is far below trial adherence, and the benefit on ventilator days seen in trials depends on it. In the records, the process breaks down after the screen: a reminder improved documentation but not interruptions, and a value stream map found the longest wait at physician approval, whose removal was followed by a large rise in completed interruptions. Nurses describe fear of self-extubation, family presence, pressure before rounds and unclear authority. Self-extubation during interruptions is rare. Coordination of awakening and breathing trials by a shared time raised paired trials in one unit. The evidence supports a local lean redesign aimed at the waits after the screen, with self-extubation and agitation as balancing measures.
gradeRationale: Single-unit before-after reports and observational studies with a consistent direction, a review of trials that is indirect for implementation, and one interrupted time series; certainty that a redesign of the morning process raises completed interruptions is low.
summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims recorded; overall certainty low; three leads remain unverified.
